mechanisms.name: Multi-Organ Dysfunction and Failure
mechanisms.description: Critical illness often leads to dysfunction across multiple organ systems (renal, hepatic, cardiac, respiratory, neurological). Biomarkers such as creatinine (renal), bilirubin and AST (hepatic), and eGFR provide direct quantification of organ damage. Organ dysfunction worsens prognosis by disrupting homeostasis, reducing resilience to stressors, and limiting recovery potential.
mechanisms.label: Organ Dysfunction

mechanisms.name: Sepsis and Systemic Inflammatory Response
mechanisms.description: Sepsis triggers widespread inflammation, capillary leak, coagulation disturbances, and organ injury. Surviving sepsis is a major determinant of ICU outcomes. Markers such as CRP, WBC, lactic acid, and the 'Sepsis3' variable indicate systemic inflammation and bacterial burden.
mechanisms.label: Inflammatory

mechanisms.name: Acute Respiratory Distress and Hypoxemia
mechanisms.description: Dysfunction in gas exchange (e.g., ARDS, severe pneumonia) causes hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and impaired ventilatory mechanics. Variables like PaO2, FiO2, PaO2/FiO2, SpO2, respiratory rate, PEEP, and compliance represent the severity and effectiveness of respiratory support.
mechanisms.label: Respiratory

mechanisms.name: Cardiovascular Instability and Shock
mechanisms.description: Shock—whether septic, cardiogenic, or hypovolemic—results in tissue hypoperfusion and is reflected by features such as hypotension (ABP, NBPs, NBPd), central venous pressure, heart rate, requirement for vasoactive medications (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dobutamine), and blood lactate. These illustrate attempts to maintain adequate organ perfusion in the face of circulatory collapse.
mechanisms.label: Cardiovascular

mechanisms.name: Neurological Impairment and Coma
mechanisms.description: Altered consciousness due to brain injury, metabolic derangement, or excessive sedation is a predictor of adverse outcomes. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), including its eye, verbal, and motor components, captures the extent of neurological impairment.
mechanisms.label: Neurological

mechanisms.name: Metabolic Dysregulation and Electrolyte Imbalances
mechanisms.description: Critical illness is often accompanied by disturbances in glucose handling, acid-base status, and electrolytes. Features such as glucose, sodium, potassium, calcium, bicarbonate (HCO3), anion gap, pH, and base excess are essential for detecting life-threatening derangements.
mechanisms.label: Metabolic

mechanisms.name: Comorbidities and Patient Characteristics
mechanisms.description: Baseline vulnerabilities such as advanced age, gender, pre-existing diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, and obesity markedly heighten the risk of ICU mortality by reducing physiological reserves and increasing susceptibility to complications.
mechanisms.label: Patient Factors

mechanisms.name: Coagulopathy and Hematologic Abnormalities
mechanisms.description: Severe illness may induce coagulopathy (impaired clotting or excessive bleeding), anemia, or thrombocytopenia, increasing the risk of poor tissue oxygenation, bleeding, or thrombotic complications. These are reflected in values such as platelet count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, PTT, and INR.
mechanisms.label: Hematologic

mechanisms.name: Service Type and Clinical Pathways
mechanisms.description: Different ICU service types (medical, surgical, trauma, etc.) reflect both the underlying illness burden and the nature of interventions. These categories may proxy for unmeasured severity or risks intrinsic to the admitting diagnosis and relate to different mortality risks.
mechanisms.label: Clinical Pathway
